Replacing worn turf in Poinciana's earliest villages

Turf replacement in Poinciana, Florida is quoted per job after a base inspection, not a flat square-foot rate. Poinciana's original villages date to 1972, and turf converted there over the past 10 to 20 years is now old enough in places that replacement, not another repair, becomes the honest recommendation.

Reviewed by Luis Austin, owner · Last reviewed September 21, 2026

Some of the community's oldest turf is reaching the end of its window

Turf generally lasts 10 to 20 years depending on UV stabilization, traffic and infill, and lawns converted in Poinciana's first villages soon after the community's 1972 founding, or during the growth wave that followed Avatar's takeover in the mid-1980s, are now old enough that a base inspection makes more sense than another round of spot repairs. Our guide to turf lifespan in Florida covers what shortens that window on a given lot.

A full replacement is the point to correct an older base

Replacement at that stage usually means rebuilding to the current washed, open-graded standard rather than reusing whatever sat underneath the original install, since that requirement postdates a meaningful share of the turf already in Poinciana's ground. It's also the practical point to re-check a canal- or pond-adjacent layout against the state's 10-foot waterbody setback, in case the original install predates the current rule.

A base that looks flat but was never washed to begin with

An older Poinciana lawn's base can appear level and well-compacted on the surface while still holding a fines crust from subgrade material that was never washed before the original install, years before the current standard required it. That crust doesn't announce itself as a problem until the turf above it is pulled up during a replacement, at which point it's clear the base was never actually draining the way it looked like it was. Flat isn't the same as functional, which is why we check for a crust, not just for slope, before deciding a base can stay.

Staging demo so old debris doesn't contaminate a kept base

When part of a Poinciana lawn's base is solid enough to reuse, the old turf and infill coming out of the rest of the yard get staged and hauled away in a way that keeps loose material from falling back into the section being kept. Skipping this staging step risks mixing years-old, possibly crusted infill back into a base that was otherwise fine, undoing the reason for keeping it in the first place. This sequencing matters more on a replacement than a first-time install, since there's old material moving through the site that a new-build job never has to manage.

Say you have a 2011-installed lawn in Village 2

Say you have a lawn converted to turf in 2011 in Village 2, now matted flat across the high-traffic path from the driveway to the back gate, with a base that's started holding water after storms. At roughly 15 years old, that lawn sits near the upper end of a typical service life, and a replacement quote would include probing the base in more than one spot before deciding whether the rock underneath can stay or needs to come out with the old turf.

Choosing a PFAS-free product during a replacement

Florida's turf standard bars intentionally added PFAS in any new synthetic turf installation, and a Poinciana homeowner replacing an older lawn gets to choose from current product lines built to that standard rather than whatever was on the market when the original turf went in. Asking a supplier for documentation on this point during a replacement is a reasonable ask, since it's exactly the kind of material change a full re-turf is positioned to address that a smaller repair job never would be.

The village's design board reviews a replacement the same as new work

Because a full tear-out and relay counts as an exterior change under APV's or Solivita's landscaping criteria, a replacement project goes through the same DCB or ARC submittal a brand-new installation would, even though the yard has carried turf for a decade or more already. Our piece on what a turf warranty actually covers is worth reading before deciding whether a manufacturer's coverage applies to the old install.

An irrigation line capped with tape instead of properly sealed

A sprinkler line simply folded over and taped rather than cut back and capped with a proper fitting is a common shortcut on a Poinciana replacement, and tape doesn't hold against water pressure the way a sealed cap does. A line that fails this way months later can undermine the new base from below with a slow, hidden leak, the kind of problem that's invisible until a soft spot appears in turf that's only been down a short time. Confirming each line was properly capped, not just covered, is worth asking about directly.

Watching a corrected footprint for a new drainage low point

Moving a Poinciana lawn's edge outside a live oak's drip line or farther back from a setback line during replacement changes where water moves across that section of yard, even when the correction itself was overdue and necessary. The boundary where the new, adjusted footprint meets the older, unchanged part of the lawn is worth watching through the first few storms, since a grade change at that line can create a small low point that wasn't there under the old layout until the new one settles in fully.

Questions people ask

How do I know if Poinciana turf needs replacing instead of repairing?

A base inspection at more than one spot on the lawn is the reliable way to tell. Turf that's matted but sitting on a base that still drains fine can often be repaired; a base that's crusted or holding water usually means replacement.

Does a replacement project need DCB or ARC approval again?

Yes. A full tear-out and relay counts as an exterior change under either board's criteria, so it goes through the same landscaping submittal a new installation would, regardless of how long turf was already on the lot.
